title: Resource Records for the DNS Security Extensions
subtitle: The four record types that let DNS answers carry proof of where they came from.
summary: RFC 4034 defines the four resource record types that DNSSEC adds to the Domain Name System: DNSKEY holds a zone's public key, RRSIG holds a signature over a set of records, NSEC proves that a name or record type does not exist, and DS links a parent zone to a child zone's key. It specifies each record's wire format and text format, plus the canonical form and ordering that signatures are computed over. Companion documents RFC 4033 and RFC 4035 describe the goals and the validation procedure.

eli5.summary: Imagine every answer from a phone book came with a wax seal. This document describes the four kinds of seals, keys and notes that let you check a seal is real and that a missing name really is missing.

questions: what does an nsec record do
what is a ds record in dnssec
how does dnssec prove a name does not exist
what is the dnskey key tag
what are the dnssec resource record type numbers

tldr.problem: Plain DNS answers carry no proof of origin, so a resolver cannot tell a genuine answer from a forged one.
tldr.mechanism: Four new record types: DNSKEY publishes a zone's public key, RRSIG signs each set of records, NSEC chains the names in a zone to prove non-existence, and DS in the parent zone points to the child's key.
tldr.outcome: Resolvers can check signatures from a trusted starting key down through each delegation, and these formats are still the base of DNSSEC today, extended by later RFCs.

today: These record types are visible in every signed zone. Tools such as dig and delv display DNSKEY, RRSIG, NSEC and DS records, and parent zones publish DS records for signed child zones; for example, the root zone holds DS records for most top-level domains. Later RFCs update this one: RFC 6840 clarifies it and RFC 5155 adds the NSEC3 alternative to NSEC. Newer algorithms and digest types have been registered with IANA since 2005, so the Appendix A tables here are only a starting point.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
DNS answers are plain data: a resolver asks, a server replies, and nothing in the reply proves it is genuine. The DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC) add digital signatures to DNS data. RFC 4034 is the part of the DNSSEC family that defines the new resource record types needed to carry those signatures and keys.

The RFC introduces four of them: DNS Public Key (DNSKEY), Resource Record Signature (RRSIG), Next Secure (NSEC) and Delegation Signer (DS). For each it gives the purpose, the RDATA wire format and the presentation (text) format. All numeric type codes in the document are decimal.

It is one of a set that is meant to be read together. RFC 4033 introduces DNSSEC and defines its terms, and RFC 4035 defines the protocol operations, including how a validator actually uses these records. This document replaced the earlier DNSSEC specification, RFC 2535, along with several RFCs that patched it.

RFC 4034 defines only formats. How a resolver builds a chain of trust and decides an answer is secure or bogus is specified in RFC 4035.
sections.eli5: This paper describes four new kinds of labels that can be stuck on phone book entries so you can tell they are real. How to check them is explained in sister papers.

sections.title: The DNSKEY Record
sections.content:
A zone signs its authoritative record sets with a private key and publishes the matching public key in a DNSKEY record, type 48. A resolver uses that public key to check signatures. The RFC says DNSKEY must not be used to store arbitrary keys or certificates that do not directly relate to the DNS infrastructure.

The RDATA has a 2-octet Flags field, a 1-octet Protocol field, a 1-octet Algorithm field and the Public Key. Two flag bits are defined. Bit 7 is the Zone Key flag: if it is set, the key is a zone key and may verify RRSIGs. Bit 15 is the Secure Entry Point flag (from RFC 3757), a hint to signing and debugging software that validators must not use to change their behavior. All other flag bits must be zero.

The Protocol field must be 3 and a DNSKEY with any other value is invalid for verification; the field survives for compatibility with the older KEY record. In text form the flags are shown as a decimal number, which for the defined bits means 0, 256 or 257, and the key is Base64.

The RFC's example is example.com. 86400 IN DNSKEY 256 3 5 ( ... ): flags 256 (Zone Key set), protocol 3, algorithm 5 (RSA/SHA-1).
sections.eli5: A DNSKEY is like a lock that anyone can look at. The owner keeps the only key that fits it, and uses that key to put seals on their answers. Everyone else uses the lock to check the seals.

sections.title: The RRSIG Record
sections.content:
An RRSIG record, type 46, holds the digital signature for one RRset: all the records sharing a name, class and type. It says which type it covers, which algorithm made it, when it is valid, and which DNSKEY can check it, through the Signer's Name and Key Tag.

Several fields exist so a validator can rebuild exactly what was signed. Original TTL records the TTL in the authoritative zone, since caches count TTLs down. Labels counts the labels in the original owner name, not counting the root label or a leading wildcard, so a validator can tell an answer was synthesized from a wildcard. For example, www.example.com. has Labels 3 and *.example.com. has 2.

Expiration and Inception are 32-bit counts of seconds since 1 January 1970 UTC, compared with serial number arithmetic (RFC 1982), so they cannot refer to dates more than 68 years away. In text form they may also be written as YYYYMMDDHHmmSS, always exactly 14 digits.

An RRSIG must have the same class and the same TTL as the RRset it covers. Because every authoritative RRset is signed, a name with a CNAME also needs an RRSIG and an NSEC, an exception to the old rule that a CNAME is the only data at a name.
sections.eli5: An RRSIG is the wax seal on a page of answers. It says which page it covers, who sealed it, and the dates between which the seal counts.

sections.title: The NSEC Record
sections.content:
Signing what exists is not enough: a resolver also needs proof that something does not exist. The NSEC record, type 47, gives it. Each NSEC names the next owner name in the zone's canonical order that has authoritative data, and lists the record types present at its own owner name. Together the NSECs form a chain through the whole zone, and each one is itself signed. The last NSEC points back to the zone apex.

If a name falls between an NSEC's owner and its next name, it does not exist. If a type is missing from the bitmap, that type does not exist at that name. RFC 4035 describes how that proof is used.

The Type Bit Maps field splits the 16-bit type space into 256 windows. Each window present is a window number (0 to 255), a bitmap length (1 to 32 octets) and the bitmap itself, with trailing zero octets omitted. In window 0, bit 1 is type 1 (A), bit 2 is type 2 (NS), and so on.

An NSEC should have the same TTL as the SOA minimum field, in the spirit of negative caching (RFC 2308). The next name must not use DNS name compression.

A side effect of the chain is that anyone can walk it to list every name in the zone. RFC 5155 later added NSEC3 to address that.
sections.eli5: An NSEC is a note that says, "after this name, the next name in the book is that one, and here is what I have under my name." If you ask about a name that would sit in between, the note proves it is not there.

sections.title: The DS Record
sections.content:
The Delegation Signer record, type 43, links one zone to the next. It stores the key tag, algorithm number and a digest of a child zone's DNSKEY. A resolver that trusts the parent zone and authenticates the DS can then authenticate the child's DNSKEY.

The DS has the same owner name as the child's DNSKEY, but lives in the parent zone as authoritative data: the DS for example.com is stored in com, while the DNSKEY is in example.com. This is what lets trust cross a zone boundary, and RFC 4035 notes it needs special response processing.

The digest is the hash of the DNSKEY's canonical owner name followed by its RDATA: digest = digest_algorithm( DNSKEY owner name | DNSKEY RDATA ). When this RFC was written the only defined digest algorithm was SHA-1, which gives 20 octets. The referenced DNSKEY must be a zone key, with bit 7 set; otherwise neither the DS nor the key may be used for validation. In text form the digest is hexadecimal.

Where it lives
In the parent zone, as authoritative data.
What it holds
Key tag, algorithm, digest type and a digest of the child's DNSKEY.
sections.eli5: The DS is a note in the parent's book that says, "the child's lock looks like this." If the lock you find matches the note, and you trust the parent, you can trust the lock.

sections.title: Canonical Form and Key Tags
sections.content:
Signatures only work if signer and verifier hash identical bytes, so the RFC defines a canonical form. Names are ordered by comparing labels as unsigned octet strings starting from the rightmost (most significant) label, treating upper-case ASCII as lower-case. This order builds the NSEC chain.

A record's canonical form is its wire format with: every name fully expanded with no compression; the owner name lower-cased; for a listed set of types (NS, CNAME, SOA, MX, SRV, RRSIG, NSEC and others) names inside the RDATA lower-cased; a wildcard owner kept in its unexpanded form with the *; and the TTL set to its original value. Within an RRset, records are sorted by their RDATA as octet strings. A duplicate record is a protocol error.

The signature itself is computed over the RRSIG RDATA, without the Signature field, followed by the sorted canonical records.

Appendix B defines the key tag, a 16-bit value that helps a validator pick the right DNSKEY from several. For every algorithm except RSA/MD5 it is the sum of the DNSKEY RDATA taken as 2-octet groups, adding the carry once. The key tag is not unique, and two different keys can share a name, algorithm and tag, so implementations must not assume otherwise.
sections.eli5: Before sealing a page, everyone agrees to write it out the same neat way: same spelling, same order. Otherwise the seal would break just because two people wrote the same words differently.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC introduces no new IANA registrations; it records the state of existing ones. Type 43 for DS came from RFC 3658 and types 46, 47 and 48 for RRSIG, NSEC and DNSKEY from RFC 3755. The old SIG, KEY and NXT types from RFC 2535 were restricted or made obsolete, and all KEY and DNSKEY records must have protocol octet 3.

Appendix A lists the algorithms of the time. Algorithm 5, RSA/SHA-1, is mandatory; 3, DSA/SHA-1, is optional; 1, RSA/MD5, is NOT RECOMMENDED; 253 and 254 are for private algorithms. Digest type 1, SHA-1, is the only digest and is mandatory.

The security discussion is short. A DS refers to a key by digest, algorithm and tag, so an attacker would need a key that matches all three. The authors judged that with SHA-1 a serious threat at the time, which is a judgment from 2005 and not a current assessment. The key tag does not identify a key uniquely, so selecting by tag alone could pick the wrong key.

The algorithm and digest tables here are historical. Current guidance on which algorithms to use is in later RFCs and the IANA registries.
sections.eli5: The numbers for the new labels were already handed out in earlier papers. The paper also warns that the label tag is only a hint, not a name, because two keys might wear the same one.

items.text: Signature over one RRset, with validity dates and a key reference.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Bit 7 is Zone Key, bit 15 is Secure Entry Point; all others must be 0.

fields.name: Algorithm
fields.desc: Identifies the key's algorithm and the format of the Public Key field.

fields.name: Public Key
fields.desc: Variable length, algorithm-dependent key material. Drawn as one row; the real field has no fixed size.

fields.name: Type Covered
fields.desc: Type of the RRset this signature covers.

fields.name: Algorithm
fields.desc: Algorithm used to make the signature.

fields.name: Labels
fields.desc: Number of labels in the original owner name, not counting the root or a wildcard label.

fields.name: Original TTL
fields.desc: TTL of the covered RRset in the authoritative zone.

fields.name: Signature Expiration
fields.desc: Seconds since 1 January 1970 UTC, compared with serial number arithmetic.

fields.name: Signature Inception
fields.desc: Start of the validity period, same format.

fields.name: Key Tag
fields.desc: Key tag of the DNSKEY that validates this signature.

fields.name: Signer's Name
fields.desc: Variable length, uncompressed owner name of the DNSKEY; the zone's name. Drawn as a partial row.

fields.name: Signature
fields.desc: Variable length signature; format depends on the algorithm. Drawn as one row.
